Section 2.6

Training Recipe

Three phases, hyperparameters, mixed precision, and the training loss curve

TL;DR

MAI-Base-1 was trained in 3 phases: pre-training (30T tokens, 16K context), mid-training 1 (3.4T tokens, 64K context), and mid-training 2 (150B tokens, 256K context). Notable choices: 0.15 dropout (unusually high), 10:1 learning rate decay ratio (gentler than standard), attention zero-initialization to prevent early MoE imbalance, and mixed FP8/BF16/FP32 precision.

Three Training Phases

PhaseTokensContext LengthGPUsPurpose

Key Hyperparameters

Optimizer: AdamW

AdamWA widely-used optimizer that adapts learning rates per parameter and includes weight decay. β₁=0.95, β₂=0.925, ε=10⁻⁸.Learn more with reduced weight decayA regularization technique that gradually shrinks model weights toward zero during training. Prevents weights from growing too large, which can cause instability. Different weight groups can use different decay rates.Learn more on attention weights (0.01) and embedding weights (0.005) — parameters that benefit less from heavy regularization.

Learning Rate Schedule

Linear warmup over ~12B tokens, then cosine decayThe learning rate follows a cosine curve from peak to minimum. The team uses a 10:1 peak-to-minimum ratio (2×10⁻⁴ → 2×10⁻⁵), gentler than the common 100:1 ratio, because less decay improved post-RL results.Learn more from 2×10⁻⁴ to 2×10⁻⁵. The 10:1 ratio (vs. the standard 100:1) was chosen because less aggressive decay improved downstream RL performance.

DropoutA regularization technique where random neurons are temporarily disabled (set to zero) during each training step. This prevents the model from over-relying on any single neuron and forces redundant learning. A rate of 0.15 means 15% of neurons are turned off each step.Learn more: 0.15

Unusually high for modern LLMs (most use zero dropout). Applied at each layer's output before the residual addition. Found to provide complementary regularization alongside weight decay, improving performance on the scaling ladder.

Example: During each training step, 15% of the neurons in each layer are randomly "turned off" — their outputs set to zero. This forces the model to develop redundant representations rather than relying on any single pathway. If expert #203 always relied on neuron #4,517 in the previous layer for recognizing Greek mathematical symbols, dropout forces the model to also learn backup pathways through neurons #1,203 and #8,901 — so the capability survives even when any single neuron is disabled.

Batch Size: 134M tokens

Constant across all three phases. Global gradient normThe total magnitude of all gradients across the model's parameters. Clipping it to 1.0 prevents 'exploding gradients' — rare batches that produce extremely large updates which could destabilize the entire model.Learn more clipped to 1.0.

In context: 134 million tokens per batch means about 100,000 pages of text processed before each gradient update. Split across 8,192 GPUs, that's ~16,384 tokens per GPU per step — roughly one page of text each. The model processes this in a few seconds, computes gradients, and updates all ~1 trillion parameters before seeing the next batch.

Mixed Precision

Different precisions for different operations, balancing speed and numerical accuracy:

  • FP88-bit floating point — a compact number format using only 1 byte per value (vs. 4 bytes for FP32). E4M3 variant: 4 exponent bits + 3 mantissa bits, optimized for forward passes. E5M2: 5+2 bits, better dynamic range for gradients.Learn more E4M3 — forward pass GEMMsGeneral Matrix Multiplications — the core computation in neural networks. Attention and FFN layers are mostly large matrix multiplies. Custom GEMM kernels are critical for GPU performance.Learn more (matrix multiplications)
  • FP8 E5M2 — data gradients in backward pass
  • BF16Brain Float 16 — a 16-bit format with the same exponent range as FP32 but fewer mantissa bits. Widely used in LLM training as a middle ground: half the memory of FP32 with adequate precision for most operations.Learn more — weight gradients, default weights and activations
  • FP32 — numerically sensitive locations: attention scores, router logits, residual stream, embeddings, RMSNorm, optimizer state, all-reduce, gradient accumulation

Stochastic roundingA rounding method where the direction of rounding is random, with probability proportional to the distance. E.g., 3.7 rounds to 4 with 70% probability and to 3 with 30%. This preserves the expected value across many operations, reducing systematic bias from always rounding down.Learn more applied when casting gradients from higher to lower precision.

Why different precisions? FP32 can represent numbers like 3.14159265358979 (7 decimal digits of precision). FP8 E4M3 only gets ~2 digits: 3.14 becomes 3.0 or 3.25. That's fine for the bulk of matrix multiplications (a small rounding error in one of millions of multiply-adds barely matters). But for attention scores — where the difference between attending to token A vs. token B might be 0.0001 — that precision loss would corrupt the model's reasoning. So sensitive operations stay in FP32 while the heavy computation runs 4x faster in FP8.

Why BF16 over FP16? FP16 has only 5 exponent bits — its max value is 65,504. During training, gradient magnitudes can exceed this, causing overflow (NaN) and crashing the run. BF16 has 8 exponent bits (same as FP32), handling the full range up to 3.4 x 10^38. The tradeoff: BF16 has fewer mantissa bits (7 vs FP16's 10), meaning less precision per number. But neural networks are robust to this — the noise during training from dropout, batch sampling, and stochastic rounding is already larger than the precision difference.

FormatBitsSize (7B model)PrecisionRangeUsed For
FP323228 GB~7 digits+/-3.4 x 10^38Optimizer states, loss accumulation

Attention Zero-Init

A notable trick for training stability: attention output is initialized to zero (via zero RMSNorm gains). This means the model initially behaves as a stack of independent FFNs processing each token separately. Cross-token interactions from attention gradually emerge during training.

Figure 8 — Attention Initialization

(a) Random init: Attention initially performs causal mean pooling, collapsing token representations and causing extreme expert imbalance in subsequent MoE layers. (b) Zero init: MoE token distribution is well-behaved from the start, with much lower expert imbalance violation rates.

Training Loss Curve

Figure 9 — Training Loss over 30T Tokens

Raw (unsmoothed) loss curve. Several early spikes appeared — caused by expert imbalance on coding data under dropless routing — but loss recovered quickly each time. No training batches were skipped. No manual interventions were made.

Mid-training Data

Mid-training reuses the pre-training corpus (no new data sources) but re-weights toward reasoning:

  • STEM/Math → 35% (up from ~21% in pre-training)
  • Code stays at 55%
  • Background sources → 10%

Additional quality filtering: STEM documents are filtered for high technical correctness and reasoning depth (Bloom's taxonomy levelA classification of cognitive skills from simple (Remember, Understand) to complex (Analyze, Evaluate, Create). Filtering for 'Analyze' and above selects documents that require reasoning — worked proofs, multi-step derivations — rather than simple definitions or rote facts.Learn more ≥ "Analyze"). Memorization-aware epoch capping prevents overfitting on sources that the model has already heavily memorized.

Long Context Extension

Rather than training at the full 256K context length throughout (which would be impractical due to low MFUModel FLOP Utilization — fraction of theoretical GPU compute actually used for useful work. Long sequences have much lower MFU because attention scales quadratically with length, and communication overhead increases.Learn more at long sequence lengths), the team adopted a staged approach:

16K
Pre-training context
64K
Mid-training context
256K
Final context (140B tokens)

Progressive Scaling Works

An ablation compared five configurations on code NLL: mid-training runs at 16K, 32K, 64K, and 128K (1T tokens each), plus a progressive approach (32K mid-training + short 256K extension). Key finding: at 128K context, the progressive checkpoint matches the NLL of the full 1T-token 128K run, despite using far fewer tokens at long context lengths. All five converge to the same NLL at short contexts (16K-32K).

Figure — Code NLL vs. Context Length

Five configurations: mid-training at 16K, 32K, 64K, and 128K (1T tokens each), plus progressive (32K + short extension). The progressive checkpoint matches or exceeds mid-training at 128K.

Adaptation Is Remarkably Fast

During the 256K extension phase, the vast majority of NLL improvement occurs within the first 1-10% of training iterations, after which the curve plateaus. This suggests the model is not acquiring fundamentally new capabilities — it's calibrating its positional and attention mechanisms for sequence lengths not seen during earlier training. The representations needed to leverage long context are already present from pre-training.

Figure — 256K Adaptation Speed

256K code NLL during the context extension phase. Most improvement occurs within the first 1-10% of training iterations.

Retrieval Remains Robust

To test whether the model can retrieve information regardless of where it sits in the context, the team designed a controlled experiment: a 16K-token relevant prefix is pushed progressively further away from a 16K-token suffix by inserting irrelevant content between them (up to 256K total). Without long-context training, NLL degrades substantially as the relevant prefix moves further away. With the context-extended checkpoint, NLL remains nearly flat regardless of distance.

Figure — Retrieval NLL

Suffix NLL as related 16K prefix is pushed further away by irrelevant context. The long-context checkpoint maintains flat NLL; without long-context training, NLL degrades substantially.

4x Length Extrapolation

On a generative QA benchmark, the model exhibits up to 4x length extrapolation: a model trained at 32K context can answer questions correctly in contexts up to 128K tokens. Beyond the training distribution, accuracy drops disproportionately for evidence at the end of context (the out-of-distribution region). Long-context training resolves this asymmetry.

Figure — QA Accuracy vs. Context Length

Generative QA accuracy across context lengths for models trained at different maximum lengths. Models maintain accuracy well beyond their training context — up to 4x extrapolation — but quality degrades past that point.

Figure — Accuracy vs. Evidence Position

Where the answer evidence sits in the 256K context. Without long-context training, accuracy drops sharply when evidence is placed toward the end (out-of-distribution region). After training at 256K, accuracy is uniform regardless of evidence position — resolving the "lost in the middle" problem.

The staged approach (short pre-training + short extension phase) achieves the same long-context quality as expensive full-length training. The same recipe naturally extends to even longer context windows — 1M tokens or beyond — at modest compute cost.
